title: Let my people go (Exodus 5–10)
hook: bricks without straw, then plagues against a hardened heart
carry: this is the finger of God

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aaron: five excuses at the bush, and one answer under all of them. Your line was I will be with thee.

Moses and Aaron walk into Pharaoh's court and say four words: "Let my people go." Enslaved people in America would later sing them in the spiritual Go Down, Moses. Pharaoh's answer is a shrug: who is this Lord, that I should listen to him? I don't know him. Then he does something any overworked employee would recognize. He raises the quota. Same number of bricks every day, he orders, but no more straw. Go find your own.
screen: `LET MY PEOPLE GO.` → `WHO IS THIS LORD?` → `SAME BRICKS, NO STRAW.`

segments.voice: First, the bricks. The Hebrews scatter across Egypt gathering stubble, and they can't make the count. The Egyptian taskmasters beat the Hebrew foremen. The foremen go to Pharaoh and get nowhere, and on the way out they turn on Moses: you've made us stink in Pharaoh's eyes. And Moses turns to God: why did you ever send me? Things got worse the moment I spoke. Second, the plagues. Blood in the Nile. Frogs. Gnats. Flies. Sickness on the cattle. Boils. Hail. Locusts. Then darkness so thick it can be felt. Nine in these chapters; the tenth comes tomorrow. Pharaoh's magicians copy the first ones, then give up at the gnats and tell him: this is the finger of God. Third, the hard heart. Again and again Pharaoh promises to let the people go, then changes his mind when the trouble lifts. Sometimes the text says Pharaoh hardened his own heart; elsewhere, that God hardened it. Readers have long wrestled with that. Saint Augustine and Saint Thomas Aquinas taught that God doesn't put evil into anyone; when God is said to harden a heart, God withholds grace from someone who has already chosen to refuse it. Fourth, the cry. This is a story about bricks and wages and bodies, not only souls. The Catechism lists cheating workers of their wages among the sins that cry out to heaven, and Pope Leo the Thirteenth wrote a whole letter, Rerum Novarum, on the rights of workers. That teaching leans on stories like this one: God hearing the cry of people forced to work without straw.
screen: `BRICKS WITHOUT STRAW.` · `NINE PLAGUES, AND THE FINGER OF GOD.` · `A HEART THAT KEEPS HARDENING.` · `A CRY THAT REACHES HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Think of the people whose work you depend on and rarely see: whoever picked the fruit in your kitchen, sewed the shirt you're wearing, cleans the building you work in, drives the truck with your packages; some are paid fairly, and some are making bricks without straw. If you pray, pray for them by name or by work, with Moses's words, let my people go; if you don't, hold them in mind with respect.
Rerum Novarum, the letter on workers' rights by Pope Leo the Thirteenth, leaning on this very story: bricks without straw, and a cry God hears. Today's word.
Your line: this is the finger of God. Even Pharaoh's magicians could see it. Day three hundred seventy-one, in the books.

howItsDone: Catholic social teaching, beginning with Pope Leo XIII's letter Rerum Novarum in 1891, defends workers' right to a just wage, and the Catechism lists defrauding laborers of their wages among the sins that cry to heaven.

chat.says: Why would a pope's letter care about the Exodus story?
options: It's about bricks and wages, not only souls: God hears overworked people's cry.
Because Pharaoh was the first ruler the Church ever officially condemned.
Because the plagues show that strikes and protests always end in disaster.

notes: Week-end look-back (365–371) is carried in the review: Joseph's tears, the midwives, the basket, the bush.
Go Down, Moses: African American spiritual (19th century), public domain; only its refrain is referenced. Confirm the framing.
Plague list (7–10): blood, frogs, gnats (DR 'sciniphs'), flies, livestock, boils, hail, locusts, darkness; the magicians' 'finger of God' at 8:19 (DR 8:19 / Hebrew 8:15). Confirm verse numbering.

Pharaoh hardens his own heart (e.g., 8:15, 8:32) and God hardens it (9:12; 10:20, 27). Aquinas ST I-II q.79 a.3 (God as cause of spiritual blindness and hardness by withholding grace); Augustine similarly. Confirm the summary.
CCC 1867 lists 'injustice to the wage earner' among sins that cry to heaven; CCC 2434 on just wages. Confirm.
